Listening Library presents Magic Treehouse Book Number One.
Dinosaurs Before Dark by Mary Pope Osborne.
Read for you by the author.
“A real monster in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.”
said Annie, She ran up the road, Oh, brother.
This is what he got for spending time with his sevenyear-old sister, Annie loved pretend stuff.
But Jack was eight and a half.
Annie raced alone into the woods.
The sun was about to set.
Jack left the road and headed into the woods.
The trees were lit with a golden late-afternoon light.
Standing under a tall oak tree.
She was pointing at a rope ladder.
The longest rope ladder Jack had ever seen.
The ladder went all the way up to the top of the tree.
There—at the top—was a tree house.
It was tucked between two branches.
“That must be the highest tree house in the world,” said Annie.
But I’m going up,” said Annie.
We don’t know who it belongs to," said Jack.
“Just for a teeny minute,” said Annie.
Annie disappeared inside the tree house.
He was about to call again when Annie poked her head out of the tree house window.
He pushed his glasses into place.
He gripped the sides of the rope ladder, and up he went.
Jack crawled through a hole in the tree house floor.
The tree house m filled with books.
Very old books with dusty covers.
New books with shiny, bright covers.
You can see far, far away,” said Annie.
She was peering out the tree house window.
Jack looked out the window with her, Down below were the tops of the other trees.
In the distance he saw the Frog Creek library.
The elementary school, The park, Annie pointed in the other direction.
There was their white wooden house with the green porch.
Next door was their neighbor’s black dog, Henry.
“We’re not supposed to be up here.”
He glanced around the tree house again.
“I wonder who owns all these books,” he said.
He noticed bookmarks were sticking out of many of them.
She held up a book with a castle on the cover.
“Here’s a book about Pennsylvania,” said Jack, He turned to the page with the bookmark.
“Hey, there’s a picture of Frog Creek in here,” said Jack.
“Oh, here’s a book for you,” said Annie.
She held up a book about dinosaurs.
A blue silk bookmark was sticking out of it.
Jack set down his backpack and grabbed the book from her.
“You look at that one, and I’ll look at the one about castles,” said Annie.
“We don’t know who these books belong But even as he said this, Jack opened the dinosaur book to where the bookmark was, He couldn’t help himself.
He turned to a picture of an ancient flying reptile.
He touched the huge bat-like wings.
“I wish I could see a Pteranodon for real.”
Jack studied the picture of the odd-looking creature soaring through the sky.
She pointed to the tree house window.
A giant creature was gliding above the treetops!
He had a long, weird crest on the back of his head.
It was a real live Pteranodon!
The creature curved through the sky.
He was coining straight toward the tree house.
He looked like a glider plane!
Jack nearly fell out the window trying to see it.
The tree house started to spin.
She pulled him back from the window.
The tree house was still high up in an oak tree.
But it wasn’t the same oak tree.
He looked down at the picture in the book.
He looked back out the window.
The world outside and the world in the picture—they were exactly the same.
The Pteranodon was soaring through the sky.
The ground was covered with ferns and tall grass.
The Pteranodon glided down to the base of their tree.
The creature coasted to a stop.
He looked at her, “I don’t know,” said Jack.
“I was looking at the picture in the book-” “And you said, 'Wow, I wish I could see a Pteranodon for real,’ ” said Annie.
In the Frog Creek woods,” said Jack.
And then the wind got loud.
And the tree house started spinning,” said Annie.
Annie looked out the window again.
“He’s very real,” Jack looked out the window with her.
The Pteranodon was standing at the base of the oak tree.
His giant wings were spread out on either side of him.
Annie called again to the creature.
The Pteranodon looked up at them.
“But maybe the book can tell us.”
Jack looked down at the book.
He read the words under the picture: This flying reptile lived in the Cretaceous period.
They couldn’t have landed in a time 65 million years ago.
Let’s go down and talk to him.”
Annie started down the rope ladder.
She stepped boldly up to the ancient creature.
Jack gasped as Annie held out her hand.
She was always trying to make friends with animals.
But this was going too far.
“Don’t get too close to him, Annie!”
Jack shouted, But Annie touched the Pteranodon’s crest, She stroked his neck.
What in the world was she saying?
It would be good to examine the creature.
Jack started down the rope ladder.
When he got to the ground, Jack was only a few feet away from the creature.
His eyes were bright and alert.
He brushed his hand down the creature’s neck.
A thin layer of fuzz covered the Pteranodon’s skin.
Jack reached into his backpack and pulled out a pencil and a notebook.
He wrote: FUZZY SKIN “What are you doing?”
“We’re probably the first people in the whole world to ever see a real live Pteranodon.”
Jack looked at the Pteranodon again.
The creature had a bony crest on top of his head.
The crest was longer than Jack’s arm.
“I wonder how smart he is,” Jack said, “Very smart,” said Annie.
“His brain’s probably no bigger than a bean.”
I can feel it,” said Annie.
Jack wrote in his notebook; SMALL BRAIN?
Jack looked at the creature again, “Maybe he’s a mutant,” he said.
Annie leaned close to the Pteranodon.
“Do you know where we are, Henry?”
The creature fixed his eyes on Annie.
His long jaws were opening and closing.
Like a giant pair of scissors.
“Are you trying to talk to me, Henry?”
Jack wrote in his notebook: MOUTH LIKE SCISSORS?
“Did we come to a time long ago, Henry?”
“Is this a place from long ago?”
Annie was pointing toward the hill.
On top stood a huge dinosaur!
He threw his notebook into his pack.
He pushed Annie toward the rope ladder.
He gave Annie a big push.
But she started up the ladder.
They tumbled into the tree house.
They were panting as they looked out the window at the dinosaur.
He was standing on the hilltop.
“We are in a time long ago!”
The dinosaur looked like a huge rhinoceros.
Only he had three horns instead of one.
Two long ones above his eyes and one on his nose.
He had a big shield-like thing behind his head.
He pointed to a picture of a Triceratops.
He read the caption; The Triceratops lived in the late Cretaceous period, This plant-eating dinosaur weighed over 12,000 pounds.
Jack slammed the book shut, “Just plants.
“Don’t you want to take notes about him?”
asked Annie, “We’re probably the first people in the whole world to ever see a real live Triceratops.”
He shoved the dinosaur book into his pack.
He slung it over his shoulder and started down the ladder.
On the way down, Jack stopped.
He called up to Annie, “Just promise you won’t pet him.”
When they stepped off the ladder, the Pteranodon gave them a kind look.
Annie blew a kiss at him.
“Be back soon, Henry,” she said cheerfully.
And he led the way through the ferns.
When he reached the bottom of the hill, he kneeled behind a fat bush.
Annie knelt beside him and started to speak.
Jack put his finger to his lips.
Jack peeked out at the Triceratops.
He was eating the flowers off a magnolia tree.
Jack slipped his notebook out of his pack, He wrote; EATS FLOWERS Annie nudged him.
He wrote: EATS SLOWLY Annie nudged him hard.
She walked her fingers through the air.
In full view of the Triceratops!
The big dinosaur had spotted Annie.
He gazed down at her from the hilltop.
Half of a magnolia flower was sticking out of his mouth.
Jack shouted at her, “He looks nice, Jack.”
Watch out for his horns, Annie!"
But the Triceratops just gazed calmly down at Annie.
Then he turned and loped away.
Down the side of the hill.
But he wrote in his notebook: NICE “Come on.
Let’s look around some more,” said Annie.
As Jack started after Annie, he saw something glittering in the tall grass.
He reached out and picked it up.
A letter was engraved on the medallion, A fancy M.
Someone came here before us,” Jack said softly.
Annie had gone up to the hilltop.
She was busy picking a flower from the magnolia tree.
But Annie wasn’t paying attention to Jack, She was staring at something on the other side of the hill.
Clutching her magnolia flower, she took off down the hill.
“I’m going to kill her,” Jack muttered.
He stuffed the gold medallion into his jeans pocket.
Jack heard another sound as well.
Jack grabbed his backpack and raced up the hill.
When he got to the top, he gasped.
The valley below was filled with nests.
Big nests made out of mud.
And the nests were filled with tiny dinosaurs!
Annie was crouching next to one of the nests, And standing over her was a gigantic duck-billed dinosaur!
He stepped slowly down the hill toward Annie.
The huge dinosaur was towering above Annie.
He didn’t want to get too close.
Clutching her flower, Annie crawled toward Jack.
Jack inched farther down the hill.
Until he was just an arm’s distance from Annie.
He reached out—and grabbed her hand, He pulled Annie toward him.
He crouched next to her, “Bow your head.
I read that’s what you do if a mean dog comes at you.”
Jack and Annie both bowed their heads.
“I don’t think she’s mad anymore,” he said.
“Thanks, Jack, for saving me,” said Annie.
"You have to use your brain,” said Jack.
“You can’t just go running to a nest of babies.
Annie held out her magnolia flower to the dinosaur.
“I’m sorry I made you worry about your babies,” she said.
The dinosaur moved closer to Annie.
She grabbed the flower from her.
The dinosaur let out a sad tuba sound.
“But there are more flowers up there," Annie said.
She pointed to the top of the hill.
Some were crawling out of their nests.
Jack took out the dinosaur book.
He flipped through the pages, He found a picture of some duck-billed dinosaurs.
He read the caption: The Anatosauruses lived in colonies.
While a few mothers babysat the nests, others hunted for food.
So there must be more mothers close by.
Annie was at the top of the hill.
Feeding magnolia flowers to the giant Anatosaurus!
But suddenly the Anatosaurus made her terrible tuba sound.
Annie crouched down and started to chew.
The dinosaur barged down the hill.
Jack put the book down on top of his pack.
“I wonder why she ran away,” said Annie.
What he saw in the distance almost made him throw up.
An enormous ugly monster was coming across the plain.
He was walking on two big legs.
And swinging a long, thick tail.
And his jaws were wide open.
Even from far away Jack could see his long, gleaming teeth.
They dashed down the hill together.
Through the tall grass, through the ferns, past the Pteranodon, and right to the rope ladder, They scrambled up, Seconds later they tumbled into the tree house.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
He looked through the window with her.
But then the monster stopped and turned around.
The two of them hunched down.
After a long moment, they raised their heads.
“We have to get out of here,” said Jack.
“You made a wish before,” said Annie.
“I wish we could go back to Frog Creek,” said Jack.
You were looking at a picture in the dinosaur book.
I left the book and my pack on the hill.
Plus my notebook’s in my pack.
Jack hurried down the rope ladder.
He raced past the Pteranodon, through the ferns, through the tall grass, and up the hill, He looked down.
There was his pack, lying on the ground.
On top of it was the dinosaur book, But now the valley below was filled with Anatosauruses.
All standing guard around the nests.
Did fear of the Tyrannosaurus send them home?
All the Anatosauruses were bellowing at him.
He raced up to the hilltop.
And he was standing between Jack and the tree house!
Jack jumped behind the magnolia tree.
His heart was beating so fast he could hardly think.
He peeked out at the giant monster, The horriblelooking creature was opening and closing his huge jaws.
His teeth were as big as steak knives, Don’t panic.
Jack peered down at the valley.
Good, The duck-billed dinosaurs were sticking close to their nests.
Jack looked back at the pteranosaurus.
Good, The monster still didn’t seem to know he was there, Don’t panic.
Maybe there’s information in the book.
He read: Tyrannosaurus rex was the largest meat-eating land animal of all time.
If it were alive today, it would eat a human in one bite.
The book was no help at all.
He couldn’t hide on the other side of the hill.
He couldn’t run to the tree house.
Wait for the monster to leave.
The Tyrannosaurus had wandered closer to the hill.
Annie was coming down the rope ladder!
Jack watched Annie hop off the ladder.
She went straight to the Pteranodon.
She pointed at Jack, at the sky, at the tree house.
The Tyrannosaurus rex was looking in his direction.
The Tyrannosaurus rex was coming toward the hill.
Just then a giant shadow covered Jack.
The giant creature sailed down toward the top of the hill.
He was coming straight for Jack.
The Pteranodon coasted down to the ground.
He stared at Jack with his bright, alert eyes.
What was Jack supposed to do?
He was starting up the hill.
His giant teeth were flashing in the sunlight.
Jack put his book in his pack.
Then he eased down onto the Pteranodon’s back.
He spread out his wings-and lifted off the ground!
The Pteranodon steadied himself, then rose into the sky.
The Tyrannosaurus was chomping the air and staring up at him.
Over all the nests filled with babies.
Over all the giant duck-billed dinosaurs.
Then the Pteranodon soared out over the plain-over the Triceratops who was grazing in the high grass.
The wind was rushing through his hair.
The air smelled sweet and fresh.
He was riding on the back of an ancient flying reptile!
The Pteranodon sailed over the stream, over the ferns and bushes.
Then he carried Jack down to the base of the oak tree.
When they came to a stop, Jack slid off the creature’s back.
Then the Pteranodon took off again and glided into the sky.
Annie shouted from the tree house.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
He kept staring up at the Pteranodon.
“Thanks for saving my life,” he said.
The Tyrannosaurus was heading straight toward him!
He grabbed the sides and started up.
Jack scrambled into the tree house.
Suddenly something slammed against the oak tree.
The tree house shook like a leaf.
Jack and Annie tumbled into the books.
The one with the picture of Frog Creek!”
He had to find that book about Pennsylvania.
He grabbed it and tore through it, looking for the photograph of the Frog Creek woods.
"I wish we could go home," he shouted.
The tree house started to spin.
He held on tightly to Annie.
He was still pointing at the picture of the Frog Creek woods.
He peeked out the tree house window.
Outside he saw the exact same view.
The woods were lit with a golden late-afternoon light.
The sun was about to set.
No time had passed since they’d left “Ja-ack!
a voice called from the distance.
Jack saw their mother far away.
She was standing in front of their house.
Annie stuck her head out the window and shouted, "Coming!"
“We took a trip in a magic tree house,” said Annie simply.
“But it’s the same time as when we left,” said Jack.
“And how did it take us so far away?”
“You just looked at a book and said you wished we could go there,” said Annie.
“And the magic tree house took us there.”
“And who built this magic tree house?
Who put all these books here?”
"A magic person, I guess," said Annie.
He reached into his pocket and pulled out the gold medallion.
Look, there’s a letter M on it.”
“You think M stands for magic person?”
“I just know someone went to that place before us.”
Annie poked her head out the window.
Jack put the gold medallion back in his pocket.
He pulled the dinosaur book out of his pack And put it back with all the other books, Then he and Annie took one last look around the tree house.
Jack slung his backpack over his shoulder.
Seconds later they hopped onto the ground and started walking out of the woods.
“No one’s going to believe our story,” said Jack.
"So let's not tell anyone," said Annie.
“He’ll say it was a dream,” said Annie.
“My teacher won’t believe it," said Jack.
“We better not tell anyone,” said Jack.
“I think I’m starting to not believe it myself,” he said.
They left the woods and started up the road toward their house.
As they walked past all the houses on their street, the trip to dinosaur time did seem more and more like a dream.
Only this world and this time seemed real.
He felt the engraving of the letter M.
He couldn’t explain what had happened today.
But he knew for sure that their trip in the magic tree house had been real.
“Tomorrow," Jack said softly, “we’ll go back to the woods.”
“And we’ll climb up to the tree house," said Jack.
“And we’ll see what happens next,” said Jack, “Of course,” said Annie.
And they took off together, running for home.

Jack couldn't sleep. He put his glasses on.
He looked at the clock. Five thirty.
Too early to get up. Yesterday so many strange things had happened.
Now he was trying to figure them out. He turned on the light.
He picked up his notebook. He looked at the list he'd made before going to bed.
Found tree house in woods. Found lots of books in it.
Pointed to Taranodon picture in book.
Made a wish. Went to time of dinosaurs.
Pointed to a picture of Frog Creek woods.
Made a wish. Came home to Frog Creek.
Jack pushed his glasses into place. Who was going to believe any of this?
Not his mom or his dad or his third grade teacher Miss Watkins.
Only his seven year old sister Annie. She'd gone with him to the time of the dinosaurs.
Can't you sleep? It was Annie standing in his doorway.
Said Annie. What are you doing? She walked over to Jack and looked at his notebook.
She read the list. Aren't you going to write about the gold medal? She asked.
You mean the gold medallion? Said Jack. He picked up his pencil and wrote.
Found this in dinosaur time. Aren't you going to put the letter M on the medal?
Said Annie. Medallion said Jack, not medal. He added an M.
Aren't you going to write about the magic person? Said Annie.
We don't know for sure if there is a magic person. Said Jack.
Well someone built a treehouse in the woods. Someone put the books in it.
Someone lost a gold medal in dinosaur time. Medallion said Jack for the third time.
And I'm just writing the facts. The stuff we know for sure.
Let's go back to the treehouse right now. Said Annie.
And find out if the magic person is a fact.
Are you nuts? Said Jack. The sun's not even up yet.
Come on. Said Annie. Maybe we can catch them sleeping.
I don't think we should. Said Jack. He was worried.
What if the magic person was mean? What if he or she didn't want kids to know about the treehouse?
Well I'm going. Said Annie. Jack looked out his window at the dark grey sky.
It was almost dawn. He sighed.
Okay. Let's get dressed. I'll meet you at the back door. Be quiet.
Yay. Whispered Annie. She tiptoed away as quietly as a mouse.
Jack put on jeans, a warm sweatshirt, and sneakers.
He tossed his notebook and pencil in his backpack.
He crept downstairs. Annie was waiting by the back door.
She shined a flashlight in Jack's face.
Ta-da! A magic wand! She said.
Shh! Don't wake up Mom and Dad. Whispered Jack.
And turn that flashlight off. We don't want anyone to see us.
Annie nodded and turned it off. Then she clipped it onto her belt.
They slipped out the door into the cool early morning air.
Crickets were chirping. The dog next door barked.
Henry stopped barking. Animals always seemed to do what Annie said.
Let's run, said Jack. They dashed across the dark wet lawn
and didn't stop until they reached the woods.
“We need the flashlight now,” said Jack.
Annie took it off her belt and switched it on.
Step by step, she and Jack walked between the trees.
said Annie, shining the flashlight in Jack’s face.
Annie shined her flashlight over the tops of the trees.
At the top of the tallest tree in the woods.
Annie shined her light at the tree house, and then down the tall ladder.
All the way to the ground.
She gripped the flashlight and began to climb.
What if someone was in the tree house?
Jack was alone in the dark.
Then he thought about all the books in the tree house.
When he was nearly to the tree house, he saw light in the distant sky.
He crawled through a hole in the floor and took off his backpack.
It was dark inside the tree house.
Annie was shining her flashlight on the books scattered about.
She stopped the light on a dinosaur book.
It was the book that had taken them to the time of the dinosaurs.
How could anyone forget seeing a real live Tyrannosaurus rex?
The light fell on a book about Pennsylvania.
A red silk bookmark stuck out of it.
That was the picture that had brought them home.
The light was shining on a book about knights and castles.
There was a blue leather bookmark in it.
Annie turned to the page with the bookmark.
There was a picture of a knight on a black horse.
He was riding toward a castle.
"Annie closed that book," said Jack. "I know what you're thinking."
“We wish we could see this guy for real,” Annie said.
It sounded like a horse neighing.
They both went to the window.
Annie shined the flashlight down on the ground.
Then the wind began to moan.
And the tree house started to spin.
The air was damp and cool.
The sound of a horse’s whinny came again from below.
She was still holding the castle book.
A huge castle loomed out of the fog.
The tree house was in a different oak tree.
And down below, the knight on the black horse was riding by.
"We can't stay here," said Jack. "We have to go home and make a plan first."
“We have to go home and make a plan first.”
He picked up the book about Pennsylvania.
He opened it to the page with the red silk bookmark.
He pointed to the photograph of the Frog Creek woods.
She yanked the book away from him.
I want to visit the castle!”
We have to examine the situation,” said Jack.
She clipped the flashlight to her belt.
And she scooted down the ladder.
Besides, he sort of wanted to take a peek himself.
He put down the book about Pennsylvania.
He dropped the castle book into his pack.
And headed down into the cool, misty air.
Annie was under the tree, looking across the foggy ground.
“The knight’s riding toward that bridge, I think,” said Annie.
I’ll look it up,” said Jack.
He took the flashlight from her and pulled the castle book out of his pack.
He opened it to the page with the leather bookmark.
He read the words under the picture of the knight: This is a knight arriving for a castle feast.
Knights wore armor when they traveled long and dangerous distances.
A helmet alone could weigh up to forty pounds.
Jack had weighed forty pounds when he was five years old.
So it’d be like riding a horse with a fiveyear-old on your head.
He wanted to take notes, as he’d done on their dinosaur trip.
He turned the pages of the castle book.
He found a picture that showed the whole castle and the buildings around it.
“The knight’s crossing the bridge,” said Annie.
“He’s going through the gate .… He’s gone.”
Jack studied the bridge in the picture.
He read: A drawbridge crossed the moat.
The moat was filled with water, to help protect the castle from enemies.
Some people believe crocodiles were kept in the moat.
said Annie, peering through the mist.
“Yeah, there’s a windmill in here, too,” said Jack, pointing at the picture.
“Look at the real one, Jack,” said Annie.
A piercing shriek split the air.
“It sounded like it came from that little house over there!”
“There’s a little house here,” said Jack, studying the picture.
He turned the page and read: The hawk house was in the inner ward of the castle.
Hawks were trained to hunt other birds and small animals.
Jack wrote in his notebook: “We must be in the inner ward,” said Jack.
He turned more pages of the book.
“I want to see what’s really going on, Jack.
Not what’s in the book,” said Annie.
He pointed to a picture of a big party.
Men were standing by the door, playing drums and horns.
He read: Fanfares were played to announce different dishes in a feast.
Feasts were held in the Great Hall.
I’m going to the real feast,” said Annie.
It showed boys his age carrying trays of food.
Jack wrote: He held up the book to show Annie.
“Look, I think they eat—” Where was she?
He heard the real drums and the real horns.
He saw the real hawk house, the real windmill, the real moat.
He saw Annie dashing across the real drawbridge.
Then she vanished through the gate leading to the castle.
“I’m going to kill her,” muttered Jack.
He threw his stuff into his pack and moved toward the drawbridge.
He hoped no one would see him.
When he got to the bridge, he started across.
The wooden planks creaked under his feet.
He peered over the edge of the bridge.
Were there any crocodiles in the moat?
A guard on top of the castle wall was looking down.
He ran through the castle gate and into the courtyard.
From inside the castle came the sounds of music, shouting, and laughter.
Jack hurried to a dark corner and crouched down.
He shivered as he looked around for Annie.
Torches lit the high wall around the courtyard.
Two boys led horses that clopped over the gray cobblestones.
It was the knight’s black horse!
She was hiding behind a well in the center of the courtyard.
He waited till the boys and horses disappeared inside the stable.
Then he dashed to the well.
They tiptoed together across the cobblestones.
Then they slipped into the entrance of the castle.
Noise and music came from a bright room in front of them.
They stood on one side of the doorway and peeked in.
He held his breath as he stared in awe.
A giant fireplace blazed at one end of the noisy room.
Antlers and rugs hung on the stone walls.
Boys in short dresses carried huge trays of food.
Dogs were fighting over bones under the tables.
People in bright clothes and funny hats strolled among the crowd.
Some tossed balls in the air.
Some balanced swords on their hands.
Men and women dressed in capes and furs sat at long, crowded wooden tables.
“I wonder which one is the knight,” said Jack.
A man carrying a tray of pies was standing a few feet away.
Then they ran as fast as they could down a dimly lit hallway.
Annie dashed toward a door off the hallway.
The two of them stumbled into a dark, cold room.
The door creaked shut behind them.
Jack handed it to her, and she switched it on.
A row of knights right in front of them!
Annie turned the light back on.
“Let me have the flashlight a second,” said Jack.
“So I can look in the book.”
He pulled out the castle book.
He flipped through the pages until he found what he was looking for.
“It’s where armor and weapons are stored.”
He shined the flashlight around the room.
The light fell on shiny breastplates, leg plates, arm plates.
On shelves filled with helmets and weapons.
On shields, spears, swords, crossbows, clubs, battle-axes.
There was a noise in the hall.
“I’ve got to check on something first.”
“It’ll take just a second,” said Jack.
He tried to lift a helmet from a shelf.
He bent over and dragged the helmet over his head.
It was worse than having a five-year-old on your head.
More like having a ten-year-old on your head.
Not only could Jack not lift his head, he couldn’t see anything, either.
Jack’s voice echoed inside the metal chamber.
He struggled to get the helmet off.
Suddenly he lost his balance and went crashing into other pieces of armor.
The metal plates and weapons clattered to the floor.
Jack lay on the floor in the dark.
But his head was too heavy.
Someone grabbed him by the arm.
The next thing he knew, his helmet was yanked off.
He was staring into the blazing light of a fiery torch.
In the torchlight, Jack saw three huge men standing over him.
One with very squinty eyes held the torch.
One with a very red face held Jack.
And one with a very long mustache held on to Annie.
said the one with the very long mustache.
said the one with the very red face.
The guards marched Jack and Annie out of the armory.
said a guard, giving him a push.
Down they marched, down the long, dark hallway.
Squinty, Annie, Mustache, Jack, and Red.
Jack heard Annie shouting at the guards.
They didn’t take her seriously at all.
At the bottom of the stairs was a big iron door with a bar across it.
Squinty pushed the bar off the door.
Then he shoved at the door.
Jack and Annie were pushed into a cold, clammy room.
The fiery torch lit the dungeon.
There were chains hanging from the filthy walls.
Water dripped from the ceiling, making puddles on the stone floor.
It was the creepiest place Jack had ever seen.
“We’ll keep them here till the feast is done.
Then turn them over to the Duke,” said Squinty.
“He knows how to take care of thieves.”
“There will be a hanging tomorrow,” said Mustache.
“If the rats don’t get them first,” said Red.
Jack saw that Annie had his backpack.
“Come on, let’s chain the two of ’em,” said Squinty.
Annie whipped her flashlight out of the pack.
They stared at the shiny flashlight in her hand.
They jumped back against the wall.
It fell into a dirty puddle on the floor, sputtered, and went out.
Annie fiercely pointed her light at one, then the other.
Each howled and covered his face.
One by one, the guards lay down on the wet floor.
Jack looked at the open doorway.
He looked at the guards quaking on the ground.
In one quick leap, Jack followed her out of the terrible dungeon.
Annie and Jack raced back up the winding stairs and down the long hallway.
They hadn’t gone far when they heard shouting behind them.
He shoved open a door off the hallway and pulled Annie into a dark room.
Then Annie shined her flashlight around the room.
There were rows of sacks and wooden barrels.
“I’d better look in the book,” said Jack.
Annie gave him the flashlight and his backpack.
He pulled out the book and started tearing through it.
Jack and Annie jumped behind the door as it creaked open.
A light from a torch danced wildly over the sacks and barrels.
His hands were trembling as he flipped through the pages of the castle book.
“Here’s a map of the castle,” he said.
“Look, this must be the room we’re in.
Jack studied the room in the book.
“These are sacks of flour and barrels of wine.”
"Here's a trap door," he read aloud.
He read aloud: This door leads from the storeroom through a secret passage to a precipice over the moat.
“But first we have to find the door.”
Jack looked at the picture carefully.
Then he shined the flashlight around the room.
The floor of the room was made up of stones.
The trapdoor in the picture was five stones away from the door to the hall.
Jack shined the light on the floor and counted the stones.
He stamped on the fifth stone.
He put the flashlight on the floor.
He worked his fingers under the thin sheet of stone and tried to lift it.
Annie came over and helped him lift the stone square out of its place.
Underneath was a small wooden door.
Jack and Annie tugged on the rope handle of the door.
The door fell open with a thunk.
Jack picked up the flashlight and shined it on the hole.
He clipped on the flashlight and felt his way down the small ladder.
When they both reached the bottom of the ladder, Jack shined the light around them.
He crouched down and began moving through the damp, creepy tunnel.
The flashlight barely lit the stone walls.
The light got dimmer and dimmer.
He was desperate to get out of the castle before the batteries died completely.
Soon he reached another small wooden door.
The door at the end of the tunnel!
Jack unlatched the door and pushed it open.
He couldn’t see anything in the misty darkness.
But I think we’ve come to the outside of the castle,” said Jack.
Jack put the flashlight in his pack.
He put the pack on his back.
He stuck his hand out the door.
“I’m going to have to go feet first,” he said.
Jack turned around in the small tunnel.
He lay down on his stomach.
He stuck one leg out the door.
Jack inched down, bit by bit.
Until he was hanging out the door, clinging to the ledge.
Water filled Jack’s nose and covered his head.
He grabbed them just in time.
He coughed and flailed his arms.
He tried to tread water and put his glasses back on.
With his backpack, his shoes, and his heavy clothes, he could hardly stay afloat.
Jack dog-paddled through the cold black water.
At first it seemed as if she was swimming in front of him.
But then he heard a splash behind him.
Her voice came from in front.
He couldn’t see anything through his water-streaked glasses.
Jack swam through the dark toward her voice.
He imagined a crocodile slithering after him.
Jack’s hand touched a wet, live thing.
She pulled him to the edge of the moat.
They crawled over an embankment onto the wet grass.
Another splash came from the moat waters.
He shook the water off his glasses and put them back on.
It was so misty he couldn’t see the castle.
He couldn’t even see the moat, much less a crocodile.
He peered at the foggy darkness.
Everything had been swallowed up by the thick, soupy darkness.
Jack reached into his wet backpack and pulled out the flashlight.
But in the still, cold darkness.
A full moon was shining in the sky.
A pool of light spread through the mist.
Then Jack and Annie saw him just a few feet away.
He sat on the black horse.
His armor shone in the moonlight.
But he seemed to be staring straight at Jack and Annie.
The knight held out his gloved hand.
“He wants to help us,” said Annie.
The knight picked Annie up and put her on the back of his horse.
Jack moved slowly toward the knight.
The knight picked him up, too.
He placed Jack on the horse, behind Annie.
The knight got on behind them.
The black horse cantered beside the moonlit water of the moat.
Jack rocked back and forth in the saddle.
He felt very brave and very powerful.
He felt as if he could ride forever on this horse, with this mysterious knight.
A hawk shrieked in the darkness.
She pointed toward a grove of trees.
The knight steered the horse toward the trees.
There it is,” Annie said, pointing to the ladder.
The knight brought his horse to a stop.
He dismounted and helped Annie down.
The knight got back on his horse.
Then he slapped the reins and rode off through the mist.
Annie started up the tall ladder, and Jack followed.
They climbed into the dark tree house and looked out the window.
The knight was riding toward the outer wall.
They saw him go through the outer gate.
Clouds started to cover the moon again.
For a brief moment, Jack thought he saw the knight’s armor gleaming on the top of a hill beyond the castle.
The clouds covered the moon completely.
And a black mist swallowed the land.
Jack shivered in his wet clothes as he kept staring at the blackness.
Jack heard Annie fumble in the darkness.
He kept looking out the window.
“I think this is it,” said Annie.
He was hoping to see the knight’s armor gleam again in the distance.
I’m going to use this,” said Annie.
“Because I think it’s the right one.
I wish we could go to Frog Creek!”
Jack heard the wind begin to blow.
“I hope I pointed to the right picture in the right book,” said Annie.
The tree house began to rock.
The wind got louder and louder.
“I hope it wasn’t the dinosaur book!”
Jack shouted at the tree house.
The tree house started to spin.
They both looked out the tree house window.
In the distance, streetlights lit their street.
There was a light on in their upstairs window.
“I think Mom and Dad are up.
In a daze, Jack unzipped his backpack.
He pulled out the castle book.
But Jack placed it back with all the other books.
said Annie, scooting out of the tree house.
Jack followed her down the ladder.
They reached the ground and took off between the gray-black trees.
They left the woods and ran down their deserted street.
They got to their yard and crept across the lawn.
Right up to the back door.
Jack and Annie slipped inside the house.
He led the way up the stairs and down the hall.
No sign of his mom or dad.
But he could hear water running in the bathroom.
Their house was so different from the dark, cold castle.
So safe and cozy and friendly.
Annie stopped at her bedroom door.
She gave Jack a smile, then disappeared inside her room.
He took off his damp clothes and pulled on his dry, soft pajamas.
He sat down on his bed and unzipped his backpack.
He took out his wet notebook.
He felt around for the pencil, but his hand touched something else.
Jack pulled the blue leather bookmark out of his pack.
It must have fallen out of the castle book.
Jack held the bookmark close to his lamp and studied it.
The leather was smooth and worn.
For the first time Jack noticed a letter on the bookmark.
Jack opened the drawer next to his bed.
He took out the gold medallion.
He looked at the letter on it.
Now this was an amazing new fact.
The person who had dropped the gold medallion in the time of the dinosaurs was the same person who owned all the books in the tree house.
Jack placed the bookmark next to the medallion.
He turned to the least wet page in his notebook.
And he started to write down this new fact.
But before he could draw the M, his eyes closed.
He dreamed they were with the knight again.
All three of them riding the black horse through the cool, dark night.
Beyond the outer wall of the castle.
And up over a moonlit hill.

It's still here, said Jack. It looks empty, said Annie.
Jack and his seven-year-old sister gazed up at a very tall oak tree.
At the top of the tree was a tree house.
Late morning sunlight lit the woods. It was almost time for lunch.
"I heard a noise," Jack said. He looked around.
"I didn't hear anything," said Annie. "Come on. Let's go up."
She grabbed onto the rope ladder and started climbing.
Jack tiptoed over to a clump of bushes. He pushed aside a small branch.
"Hello?" he said. "Anybody there?" There was no answer.
"Come on," Annie called down. "The treehouse looks the same as it did yesterday."
Jack still felt that someone was nearby.
Could it be the person who'd put all the books in the treehouse?
"Jack!" Jack gazed over the top of the bushes.
Was the mysterious person watching him now the person whose name began with M?
Maybe M wanted the gold medallion back, the one Jack had found on their dinosaur adventure.
Maybe M wanted the leather bookmark back, the one from the castle book.
There was an M on the medallion and an M on the bookmark.
But what did M stand for?
"Tomorrow I'll bring everything back," Jack said loudly.
A breeze swept through the woods. The leaves rattled.
"Come on," called Annie. Jack went back to the big oak tree.
He grabbed onto the rope ladder and climbed up.
At the top he crawled through a hole in the wooden floor.
He tossed down his backpack and pushed his glasses into place.
"Hmm, which book is it going to be today?" said Annie.
She was looking at the books scattered around the treehouse.
Annie picked up the book about castles.
"Hey, this isn't wet anymore," she said.
"Let me see." Jack took the book from her.
He was amazed. It looked fine.
Yesterday it had gotten soaked in a castle moat.
The castle book had taken Jack and Annie back to the time of nights.
Jack silently thanked the mysterious knight who had rescued them.
She waved a dinosaur book in Jack's face. "Put that away," said Jack.
The day before yesterday, the dinosaur book had taken them to the time of dinosaurs.
Jack silently thanked the pteranodon who had saved him from a Tyrannosaurus Rex.
Annie put the dinosaur book back with the other books.
She held up a book about ancient Egypt.
Jack caught his breath. He took the book from her.
A green silk bookmark stuck out of it.
Jack turned to the page with a bookmark.
There was a picture of a pyramid.
Going toward the pyramid was a long parade.
Four huge cows with horns were pulling a sled.
On the sled was a long gold box.
Many Egyptians were walking behind the sled.
At the end of the parade was a sleek black cat.
He wanted to study the book a bit more.
Pyramids were high on his list of favorite things.
He didn’t have to worry about being eaten by a pyramid.
In case we want to come right back here.”
Annie found the book with the picture of their hometown in it.
Then Jack pointed to the pyramid picture in the Egypt book.
He cleared his throat and said, “I wish we could go to this place.”
Jack looked out the tree house window.
A black cat was perched on a branch.
The cat was staring at Jack and Annie.
It was the strangest cat Jack had ever seen.
He was very sleek and dark.
“It’s the cat in the Egypt book,” whispered Annie.
Just then the wind started to blow.
Jack closed his eyes as the tree house started to spin.
Hot bright sunlight nearly blinded him.
Jack and Annie looked out the window.
The tree house was perched on the top of a palm tree.
The tree stood with other palm trees.
A patch of green surrounded by a sandy desert.
The black cat was sitting at the base of the tree.
His yellow eyes were staring up at Jack and Annie.
The black cat stood and began walking around the tree.
She leaned out the window to see where the cat was going.
Jack leaned forward and looked down.
The cat was running away from the palm trees.
Toward a giant pyramid in the desert.
A parade was going toward the pyramid.
The same parade as in the Egypt book.
Jack looked down at the Egypt book.
He read the words under the picture: When a royal person died, a grand funeral procession took place.
Family, servants, and mourners followed the coffin.
The coffin was called a sarcophagus.
It was pulled on a sled by four oxen.
“The box is called a sar … sar … sar … oh, forget it.”
The coffin called sarcophagus. "We'd better hurry," said Annie. "If we want to see the mummy."
She started down the rope ladder.
Jack looked up from his notebook.
“There’s probably a mummy in that gold box,” Annie called up.
She sure knew how to get to him.
Jack shoved his notebook and the Egypt book into his pack.
Then he started down the ladder.
When he got to the ground, he and Annie took off across the sand.
But as they ran a strange thing happened.
The closer they got to the parade, the harder it was to see it.
But the great stone pyramid was still there.
There’s no such thing as ghosts,” said Jack.
It happens in the desert all the time,” said Jack.
But it just turns out to be the sunlight reflecting through heat.”
“How could sunlight look like people, a mummy box, and a bunch of cows?”
Near the base was the sleek black cat.
He was staring at Jack and Annie.
The cat started to slink away.
He walked along the base of the pyramid and slid around a corner.
They dashed around the corner—just in time to see the cat disappear through a hole in the pyramid.
He and Annie peeked through the hole.
He pulled out the Egypt book and turned to the section on pyramids.
He read the caption aloud: Pyramids were sometimes called Houses of the Dead.
They were nearly all solid stone, except for the burial chambers deep inside.
To the burial chambers,” said Annie.
Then he stepped out of the hot, bright sunlight into the cool, dark pyramid.
The floor slanted up from where they stood.
“We have to go farther inside,” said Annie.
She gave him a little push.
Jack started up the slanting floor of the hallway.
The hallway went on and on.
“I want to look at the book.”
He opened the Egypt book again.
He held it below a torch on the wall.
The book showed a picture of the inside of the pyramid.
“The burial chamber is in the middle of the pyramid.
Jack tucked the book under his arm.
Then they headed deeper into the pyramid.
“I think we’re almost at the burial chamber.
Then you come to the chamber.
A strange cry shot through the pyramid.
Out of the shadows flew a white figure.
The white figure moved swiftly past them.
"A mummy!" said Annie. "Back from the dead!"
He picked up the Egypt book.
She lifted something from the floor.
A dog’s head was carved on one end.
“It looks like a scepter,” said Jack.
"It looks like a scepter," said Jack. "What's that?" asked Annie.
“It’s a thing kings and queens carry,” said Jack.
“It means they have power over the people.”
“But the mummy—” “That was no mummy,” said Jack.
“What kind of person would be inside a pyramid?”
At last he found a picture of a person in a pyramid.
He read: Tomb robbers often carried off the treasure buried with mummies.
False passages were sometimes built to stop the robbers.
“Yeah, a robber who steals stuff from tombs.”
“But what if the robber comes back,” said Annie.
“But first I want to write something down.”
He put the Egypt book into his pack.
He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
He started writing in his notebook: “Jack—” said Annie.
"Jack?" said Annie. "Just a second," said Jack.
Jack felt a whoosh of cold air.
A wave of terror went through him.
Another figure was moving slowly toward them.
She wore flowers in her black hair.
Her long white dress had many tiny pleats.
She handed him the gold scepter.
The lady stopped in front of them.
The scepter passed right through the lady’s hand.
The scepter passed right through the lady's hand. She was made of air.
But Jack could only stare in horror.
She spoke in a hollow, echoing voice.
Is it true that you have come to help me?”
“For a thousand years,” said the ghost-queen, “I have waited for help.”
Jack’s heart was pounding so hard he thought he might faint.
“Someone must find my Book of the Dead,” she said.
“I need it to go on to the Next Life.”
“Why do you need the Book of the Dead?”
She didn’t sound scared at all.
“It will tell me the magic spells I need to get through the Underworld,” said the ghost-queen.
“Before I journey on to the Next Life, I must pass through the horrors of the Underworld.”
“My brother hid the Book of the Dead.
So tomb robbers would not steal it,” said the ghost-queen.
“Then he carved this secret message on the wall, telling me how to find it.”
“Alas, my brother forgot my strange problem.
I cannot see clearly that which is close to my eyes.
I have not been able to read his message for a thousand years.”
“Oh, that’s not a strange problem,” said Annie.
The ghost-queen stared in wonder at Jack.
“Jack, lend her your glasses,” said Annie.
Jack took his glasses off his nose.
He held them out to the ghost-queen.
“I fear I cannot wear your glasses, Jack,” she said.
“But perhaps you will describe the hieroglyphs on these walls,” said the ghost-queen.
said Jack, finally finding his voice.
“It’s the ancient Egyptian way of writing.
Then he stepped toward the wall and took a good long look.
Chapter 6 The Writing on the Wall
Jack and Annie squinted at the pyramid wall.
A series of tiny pictures were carved into the stone.
“There are four pictures here,” Jack told the ghostqueen.
One at a time, please,” she said.
"Okay," he said. "The first one is like this."
He made a zigzag in the air with his finger.
“The second one has a long box on the bottom,” he said.
He drew it in the air.
She drew squiggly lines in the air.
More like a boat,” said Annie.
Jack took another look at the wall.
It could be a boat,” he said.
Jack and Annie studied the next picture.
“The third one is like a thing that holds flowers,” said Annie.
“Or a thing that holds water,” said Jack.
Jack and Annie studied the last picture.
“And the last one looks like a pole that droops,” said Annie.
“But one side is shorter than the other.”
Jack put down the scepter and got out his pencil.
“But that is the hieroglyph for a folded cloth,” said the ghost-queen.
He looked at the fourth hieroglyph again.
He still couldn’t see the folded cloth.
Unless it was like a towel hanging over a bathroom rod.
“So that’s all of them,” said Annie.
Jack wrote the words in his notebook.
Jack put the scepter and his notebook and pencil into his pack.
He and Annie followed the ghost-queen.
Until they came to some stairs.
The ghost-queen floated up the stairs.
The ghost-queen floated right through a wooden door.
Jack and Annie pushed on the door.
They stepped into a cold, drafty room.
The ghost-queen was nowhere in sight.
Dim torchlight lit the huge room.
It had a very high ceiling.
On one side was a pile of tables, chairs, and musical instruments.
On the other side of the room was a small wooden boat.
“What’s it doing inside Queen Hutepi’s pyramid?”
“Maybe it’s supposed to carry her to the Next Life,” said Jack.
He and Annie went over to the boat.
The boat was filled with many things.
He reached into the boat and lifted out a clay jug.
Jack felt down inside the jug.
“It feels like a big napkin,” he said.
Jack reached into the jug and pulled out the folded cloth.
It was wrapped around an ancient-looking scroll.
It was covered with wonderful hieroglyphs.
Jack traced his finger over the scroll.
It felt like very old paper.
We found your Book of the Dead!”
Then another door on the other side of the chamber creaked open.
Cold air was coming through the open doorway.
“She’s waited a thousand years for her book.
Jack put the ancient scroll into his backpack.
Then he and Annie slowly started to cross the drafty room.
They came to the open door.
Jack stepped into the other room.
Except for a long gold box.
The cover was on the floor.
There was still no sign of the ghost-queen.
“Let’s leave the scroll on the floor.
I think we should leave it in there,” said Annie.
She pointed to the gold box.
Annie took Jack by the arm.
They stopped in front of the box.
Bandages were still wrapped around the bald skull.
But most of the bandages had come off the face.
Plus the rotting bandages on her body were coming off.
She started out of the room.
She was standing by the door.
Jack pulled out the Egypt book and flipped to a picture of a mummy.
He read aloud: Ancient Egyptians tried to protect the body so it would last forever.
First it was dried out with salt.
He kept reading: Next it was covered with oil.
Then it was wrapped tightly in bandages.
She dashed out of the room.
“We have to give her the Book of the Dead!”
He pulled out the scroll and the scepter.
He put them next to the mummy’s skull.
Or did a deep sigh seem to shudder throughout the room?
Did the mummy’s face grow calmer?
Jack held his breath as he backed away.
At the bottom of the stairs, he heaved his own sigh.
Where in the world was Annie?
Had she run out of the pyramid?
He was running away from her voice.
He went back toward the burial chambers.
He went back into the boat room.
Right next to the door he had just come through.
He found himself at the top of some stairs.
They were just like the stairs in the other hallway.
He went down into the hallway.
It was lit by torches on the wall.
It was just like the other hallway.
She was running through the hallway toward him.
“I think this is one of those false passages.
Built to fool the tomb robbers,” said Jack.
“Yeah, it looks just like the right hallway,” said Jack.
“We have to go back into the boat room.
Just then they heard a creaking noise.
Then they watched in horror as the door slowly creaked shut.
A deep sound rumbled in the distance.
And all the torches went out.
“We have to get out of here fast.
“Good idea,” said Annie in a small voice.
They felt their way through the darkness.
To the top of the stairs.
Everything’s going to be okay,” said Jack.
He was trying to stay calm.
They leaned against the wooden door and pushed.
It was getting harder to breathe.
“Just … just rest a moment,” said Jack, panting.
His heart was pounding as he tried to see through the darkness.
“Maybe we should start down the hall,” he said.
“Maybe we’ll eventually come to … to an exit.”
Jack felt the stone wall as he climbed slowly down the stairs.
Jack started down the dark hallway.
It was impossible to see anything.
Taking one step at a time.
Moving his hands along the wall.
Was this the same door they had started at?
Annie took his hand in the dark.
They stood together at the top of the stairs.
"Follow him," cried Jack. "He's going away from us."
They started down the dark hallway.
Hands against the wall, Jack and Annie stumbled through the darkness.
All the way through the winding hallway.
And another … Finally they saw a light at the end of the tunnel.
They rushed forward—out into the bright sunlight.
“How did we get out of the false passage?”
“But how could the cat do it?”
Then he disappeared in the shimmering waves of heat.
Jack looked toward the palm trees.
At the top of one sat the tree house.
He and Annie set off for the palm trees.
It was a long hot walk back.
At last Annie grabbed onto the rope ladder.
Once they were inside the tree house, Jack reached for the book about Pennsylvania.
Just then he heard a rumbling sound.
The same sound they had heard in the pyramid.
Annie said, pointing out the window.
A boat was beside the pyramid.
It was gliding over the sand.
Like a boat sailing over the sea.
Or was the ghost-queen finally on her way to the Next Life?
He pointed to the picture of Frog Creek.
“I wish we could go home,” he said.
The tree house started to spin.
Late-morning sunlight shone through the tree house window.
Shadows danced on the walls and ceiling.
He was lying on the floor of the tree house.
“I wonder what Mom’s making for lunch,” said Annie.
She was looking out the window.
“I hope it’s peanut butter and jelly sandwiches,” he said.
“Boy, this place is a mess,” said Annie.
Jack had almost forgotten about M.
Would they ever meet the mysterious M?
The person who seemed to own all the books in the tree house?
“Let’s put the Egypt book on the bottom of the pile,” said Annie.
He needed a rest before he visited any more ancient tombs.
“Let’s put the dinosaur book on top of the Egypt book,” said Annie.
And a long rest before he visited another Tyrannosaurus rex.
“The castle book can go on the very top of the pile,” said Annie.
He liked thinking about the knight on the cover of the castle book.
He felt as if the knight were his friend.
She was pointing at the wooden floor.
Jack groaned as he got up.
He stood next to Annie and looked at the floor.
“Turn your head a little,” said Annie.
“You have to catch the light just right.”
Jack tipped his head to one side.
Something was shining on the floor.
He tipped his head a bit more.
This proved the tree house belonged to M.
Jack touched the M with his finger.
Then he and Annie climbed down the ladder.
As they stood on the ground below the tree house, Jack heard a sound in the bushes.
“I’m going to bring the medallion back soon,” Jack said loudly.
“I feel like M is nearby,” Jack whispered.
But just then their mother’s voice came from the distance.
Jack and Annie looked around at the trees.
Then they looked at each other.
And they took off, running out of the woods.
They ran right into their mom.
She was making peanut butter and jelly sandwiches.

She grabbed the rope ladder and started up. Jack followed.

Jack smiled. The Egypt book had taken them to the time of pyramids.

The Pennsylvania book had brought them back home at the end of each of their adventures.
Okay, he still had two main questions.

Finally Jack reached into his backpack.

Jack agreed with her. It was too wet and cold.

Annie picked up the book. She stared at the picture on the page.
She showed the picture to Jack.

Another gust of rainy wind blew into the tree house.

Sitting on a branch outside the window ledge of the tree house was a green parrot.
Exactly like the parrot in the picture.

The tree house started to spin.
Jack felt hot sunlight streaming into the tree house.
He heard the sound of waves.

The tree house was in a palm tree.

And ran across the hot sand into the waves.
The water was warm and clear.
Jack could see shells and tiny fishes.
He shielded his eyes against the sun.

The tall sailing ship seemed a bit closer.
Not over the bright blue sea.
When Jack looked out at the sea again, the ship seemed even closer.

As he stared at the ship’s flag, a chill went through him.

Jack shoved the book into his backpack.

They had pistols in their belts.
Jack started to run across the hot sand.
He ran as fast as he could.
Before Jack knew it, the biggest pirate had grabbed him!
But the pirate had huge, strong arms.
He held on to Jack and laughed a mean, ugly laugh.
He had a shaggy black beard.
He saw her coming down the rope ladder.

Together they started to back slowly away from the pirates.
He aimed his pistols at them.

“Well, it means … ” Cap’n Bones’ good eye squinted at the writing.

Cap’n Bones roared at his men.

Cap’n Bones gave Jack and Annie a dark look.
The pirate squinted his good eye.
When the treasure’s in me hands, I’ll let you go.”
"Okay," said Jack. "I'll read it to you."
“It says, The gold doth lie beneath the whale’s eye.”
“They can rot there till they’re ready to tell us how to find Kidd’s treasure!”
Jack and Annie were tossed into the rowboat.
The sky ahead was dark with thunderclouds.
A strong wind had started to blow.
Pinky and Stinky began rowing toward the big ship.
Polly the parrot was flying over the sand.
“She wants to help us,” whispered Annie.
Polly started to fly out over the waves.
But the winds were too strong.
She turned around and flew back to the island.
The rowboat tossed from side to side.
“Or we’ll be meat for those evil brutes!”
Dark fins cut through the water.

Jack could have reached out and touched it.
Soon the rowboat pulled alongside the ship.
The air was filled with wild fiddle music and bagpipes playing.
And Jack heard jeers, shouts, and ugly laughter.
"Oist 'em aboard!" Captain Bones shouted to his men.
Cap’n Bones shouted to his men.
Annie and Jack were hauled onto the deck.
It rolled from side to side.
Ropes flapped and snapped in the wild wind.
Everywhere they looked, Jack and Annie saw pirates.
A couple of pirates grabbed Jack and Annie.
And threw them in the ship’s cabin.
The air inside the cabin was damp and sour-smelling.

“We’ve got to figure out how to get back to the island.”
“So we can get into the tree house and go home,” said Annie.
How would they ever get out of this mess?
“We better examine the book,” he said.
He reached into his pack and pulled out the pirate book.
He looked for information to help them.
He found a picture of pirates burying a treasure chest.
Together they read the words under the picture.
Captain Kidd was a famous pirate.
It is said that he buried a treasure chest on a deserted island.

Annie looked out the round window.

Jack took out his notebook and pencil.
He looked back at the book.
As big as a football field.”
Jack jumped up and looked out the window with her.
All he could see was the island.
The island is shaped like a giant whale!”
The slope of the island looked like the back of a whale.
The palm tree that held the tree house looked like the spout of the whale.
A big black rock looked like the eye of the whale.
“The gold doth lie beneath the whale’s eye,” whispered Jack.
“So the treasure must be under that rock,” said Annie.
“Now we just have to get back to the island.

Then while all the pirates are digging, we’ll sneak up to the tree house.”

Jack poked his head out of the round window of the cabin.
The pirates took up the cry.
Cap’n Bones stuck his ugly face through the window.
His good eye glared at Jack.
“We’re ready to tell the truth, sir,” said Jack.
“We know where Captain Kidd’s treasure is.”
We have to show you,” said Annie.
Cap’n Bones gave Annie and Jack a long hard look.
Then he roared at his men, “Get some rope and shovels!”
“Then throw these lubbers in the boat!
We’re going back to the island!”
Back in the rowboat, Jack saw the sky had grown even darker with clouds.
“You’ll see a gale if I don’t get me gold today, by thunder!”
The three pirates battled the waves, until the rowboat reached the island.
They all piled onto the shore.
Cap’n Bones grabbed Jack and Annie.
“Now show us where the treasure is.”
She pointed at the black rock near the tip of the island.
Cap’n Bones dragged Jack and Annie down the beach to the black rock.
Cap’n Bones said to Pinky and Stinky.
How could they get away from him?
“Don’t you think you should help your friends?”
Cap’n Bones gave Jack a horrible grin.
I’m going to hold you two—till there’s treasure in me hands!”
Pinky and Stinky tied their rope around the big rock.
“Aghh, let the dogs do the work!”
“You’re not very nice to them,” said Annie.
They started pulling the rock across the sand.

Pinky and Stinky started to dig.
There was going to be a thunderstorm.
I got sand in me eyes!”
He held Jack and Annie with one hand.

He dragged Jack and Annie down the beach as he ran after his men.

Pinky and Stinky jumped into the boat.
Cap’n Bones let go of Jack and Annie.
He hauled himself into the rowboat.
Then the three pirates disappeared into the spray of the waves.
Just then the storm broke over the island.
I have to get the medallion!”
He ran to the hole dug by the pirates.

Then the rain cleared away more sand.

Was it Captain Kidd’s treasure chest?
She was halfway up the tree house ladder.
Jack kept staring at the chest.
Now Annie was shouting from the tree house window.
But Jack couldn’t tear himself away.
He brushed the rest of the muddy sand off the chest.
She was perched on the black rock.
He stared into her wise eyes.
He thought he knew her —knew her from somewhere else.
It was definitely time to go.
Jack took one last look at the treasure chest.
Then he took off, running toward the tree house.
His socks and rain boots were still there.
He quickly pulled the boots on.
He shoved the socks into his backpack.
The rope ladder was dancing wildly in the wind.
The ladder swayed as Jack climbed.
He was tossed this way and that.
At last he pulled himself into the tree house.
Annie was already holding the Pennsylvania book.
She pointed to the picture of Frog Creek.
The wind was already blowing hard.
But now it blew even harder.
The tree house started to spin.
Rain was dripping from the leaves of the tree.
They were back in Frog Creek.
He was still holding the gold medallion.
“I was hoping she might come back with us.”
“No magic creature has ever come back with us,” said Jack.
It was damp with rain and saltwater.
Jack took out the pirate book.
He put it on the stack of books.
On top of the dinosaur book.
Then Jack put the gold medallion beside the bookmark with the letter M.
Next he went down onto his knees.
And ran his finger over the shimmering M on the floor.
“We didn’t find any M’s on this trip,” he said.
The parrot swooshed into the tree house.
She perched on the stack of books.
Slowly Polly raised her bright green wings.
They grew bigger and bigger until they spread out like a huge green cape.
Then, in a great swirl of colors—in a blur of feathers and light—in a flapping and stretching and screeching—a new being took shape.
Polly was not a parrot any longer.
In her place was an old woman.
A beautiful old woman with long white hair and piercing eyes.
She wore a green feathered cape.
She perched on the stack of books.
And she was very calm and very still.
Neither Jack nor Annie could speak.
Hello, Annie,” the old woman said.
I’m the M person,” said Morgan.
“Have you ever heard of King Arthur?”
“Well, I am King Arthur’s sister,” said Morgan.
“What did you read about me, Jack?”
“You can’t believe everything you read, Jack.”
But I’m also a librarian,” said Morgan.
And I’ve come to the 20th century, your time, to collect books.
You are lucky to be born in a time with so many books.”
“I travel in this tree house to collect words from many different places around the world.
And from many different time periods.”
I want to borrow them for our scribes to copy.”
“Did you put all the bookmarks in them?”
You see, I like the pictures in the books.
Sometimes I want to visit the scenes in the pictures.
So all the bookmarks mark places I wish to go.”
“I placed a spell on the tree house,” said Morgan.
“So when I point to a picture and make the wish, the tree house takes me there.”
“I think you dropped this in dinosaur times,” said Jack.
He handed the gold medallion to Morgan.
I wondered where I’d lost it,” she said.
She put the medallion into a hidden pocket in her cape.
“You two are the only ones besides me to do it.
No one else has ever even seen my tree house before.”
“I had no idea it would ever be discovered.
But then you two came along.
Somehow you hooked right into my magic.”
“Well, for two reasons, I think,” explained Morgan.
So she actually saw the tree house.
And her belief helped you to see it, Jack.”
“Then you picked up a book, Jack.
And because you love books so much, you caused my magic spell to work.”
“You can’t imagine my dismay when you started to take off for dinosaur times.
I had to make a very quick decision.
And I decided to come along.”
“And the cat and the knight and Polly!”
“You were all these things to help us?”
“Yes, but I must go home now.
The people in Camelot need my help.”
She picked up Jack’s backpack and handed it to him.
Jack and Annie picked up their raincoats.
asked Annie, as they put their raincoats on.
She smiled at both of them.
“You remind me too much of myself.
Morgan le Fay touched Annie’s forehead gently.
Annie left the tree house first.
They climbed down the rope ladder for the last time.
They stood below the oak tree and looked up.
Morgan was looking out the window.
Her long white hair blew in the breeze.
Suddenly the wind began to blow.
A loud whistling sound filled the air.
Jack covered his ears and squeezed his eyes shut.
Annie and Jack stood a moment, staring up at the empty oak tree.
He felt too sad to speak.
As they started walking, he put his hands into his pockets.
Jack pulled out the gold medallion.
“Morgan must have put it there,” she said.
“I think it means she’ll be coming back.”
He clutched the medallion as he and Annie took off through the wet, sunny woods.
As they walked, the sun shined through the woods.
And all the wet leaves sparkled.
Leaves, branches, puddles, bushes, grass, vines, wild flowers—all glittered like jewels.
Annie had been right, thought Jack.

Jack and Annie were walking home from the library.
The path went right by the Frog Creek woods.
“Then you don’t have to come,” said Annie.
She took off into the woods.
But Annie had disappeared among the trees.
He was starting to lose hope.
Maybe he would never see Morgan again.
And there had not been one sign of Morgan le Fay.
Nor had there been one sign of her magic tree house.
Oh, she’s just pretending as usual, Jack thought.
But his heart started to race.
“She better not be kidding,” said Jack.
He took off into the woods to find Annie.
It was hard to see through the shadows.
Annie waved from the window of a tree house.
It was in the tallest oak in the woods.
A long rope ladder hung down from it.
The magic tree house was back.
Jack ran to the rope ladder.
He climbed and climbed and climbed.
As he climbed, he looked out over the woods.
High above the treetops it was still light.
At last, Jack pulled himself into the tree house.
On the floor the letter M glowed in the dim light.
The M stood for Morgan le Fay.
But there was no sign of Morgan herself.
“I wonder where Morgan is,” said Jack.
“Maybe she went to the library to get some more books,” said Annie.
We would have seen her,” said Jack.
A little mouse ran out from behind a stack of books.
It ran to the M shining in the floor.
The mouse sat on the middle of the M.
It looked up at Jack and Annie.
Jack had to admit the mouse was cute.
It had brownand-white fur and big dark eyes.
Annie slowly reached out her hand.
“Just because the mouse is in the tree house doesn’t mean it’s magic.
It’s a plain old mouse that crawled in, that’s all.”
He saw a piece of paper on the floor.
Jack went over and picked up the paper.
“Oh man,” whispered Jack, after he read the words.
I think she’s in big trouble!”
Jack showed Annie the piece of paper.
“Maybe she was trying to write things,” said Jack.
“See how the n sort of runs off the page?”
“Maybe the spell was starting to make her disappear or something,” said Annie.
“I wonder if she left any other clues.”
He glanced around the tree house.
Annie pointed at a book in the corner.
“That’s the only open book,” she said.
He felt a shiver go down his spine.
Jack went over to the book and picked it up.
He held it near the window.
Light from the setting sun was golden on the page.
Jack stared at the picture on it.
In the picture were trees with white flowers.
The trees were on the side of a mountain.
Two people were also in the picture.
They had black scarves over their faces.
And long swords strapped to their backs.
“Morgan must have left the book open to this page for a reason,” said Jack.
“Maybe that’s where she was when the spell got her,” Annie said.
“Or maybe that’s where the four things are,” said Jack.
“But we should read this book first,” said Jack.
She grabbed the book from Jack.
“We have to find out about this place.”
Annie held the book out of reach.
“We’ll find out when we get there,” she said.
“We don’t even know where there is!”
But Annie pointed at the picture.
“I wish we could go here,” she said.
The leaves of the oak tree began to shake.
Then she put it in the pouch of her sweatshirt.
The tree house started to spin.
Except for the sound of rushing water.
Annie was already looking out the window.
The mouse peeked out of her pouch.
Jack looked out the window, too.
The air was fresh and cool.
The tree house was in a tree with white flowers.
The tree was in a grove of trees on the side of a mountain.
Nearby a wild stream rushed downhill.
Two ninjas were standing on rocks near the water.
They were staring at the valley below.
They wore black pants and shirts.
They had black scarves around their heads.
And swords strapped to their backs.
It was exactly like the picture in the book.
“They might think we’re some kind of enemy,” said Jack quietly.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
Now he was going to look at the ninja book.
He read: Very little is known about the shadowy warriors called ninjas.
Historians believe that ninjas lived in Japan between the 14th and 17th centuries.
Both men and women were ninjas.
Sometimes they fought to protect their families.
Sometimes warlords hired them to be spies.
“We’re in Japan, hundreds of years ago.”
He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
I think they know we’re here.”
His eyes met the dark eyes of the tall ninja.

But where was the book about Pennsylvania?

Jack and Annie couldn’t get home without it.
He and Annie grabbed the top of the rope ladder.
They pulled the ladder into the tree house.
But the tall ninja leaped at the tree trunk.
Then he started climbing up the tree!
Jack and Annie huddled in a corner.
The ninjas climbed into the tree house.
The ninjas pulled iron bands off their hands.

The ninjas stared at Jack and Annie with dark, piercing eyes.
The rest of their faces were covered by their scarves.
Jack felt frozen under their stares.
She stepped right up to them.
They were as still as Jack.
“We’re trying to help our friend, Morgan,” said Annie.
The tall ninja took the note from her.
Then he gave it to the short ninja.
The two ninjas stared at each other.
Then they looked back at Jack and Annie.
Finally the short ninja nodded once.
He put the note into the pocket of his shirt.
Jack wished he could see their faces.
He couldn’t tell what they were thinking.
The short ninja tossed the rope ladder back out of the tree house.
The tall one pointed down the ladder.
Then he pointed at Jack and Annie.
The short ninja darted down the ladder.
His feet didn’t touch the rungs of the ladder.
The tall one did the same.
They were like spiders dropping from webs.

He looked around the tree house again.

“But I think they know something about Morgan!”
Jack put his notebook and the ninja book into his pack.
He pushed his glasses into place.
And he started down the ladder.
Jack joined Annie and the ninjas on the ground.
The sun had fallen behind the hills.
The sky was streaked with red and gold.
The mouse peeked out from Annie’s sweatshirt pouch.
But who is going to take care of us?
The short ninja held Jack’s arm in one hand and Annie’s arm in the other.
He led them through the twilight.
The tall ninja walked behind them.
The ninjas stopped near the rushing water of the wide stream.
The water roared as it raced downhill.
The short ninja looked at Jack and Annie.
He let go of their arms.
Then he pushed them toward the stream.
Then he and the short ninja stepped into the wild stream.
“Let’s run back to the tree house!”
"Let's run back to the treehouse," said Jack.

They both screamed and jumped out.
It was the coldest water Jack had ever felt!
It was so cold it felt like fire.
“I can’t go back in,” said Annie, shivering.
The ninjas looked at Jack and Annie.
Then they turned around and came back.

And put him on his shoulder.
The short ninja put Annie on his shoulder.
Then the two ninjas stepped into the stream again.

It went up to the short ninja’s waist.
But the ninjas moved through the stream as calmly as two sailing ships.

The ninjas lowered Jack and Annie to the ground.
The ninjas said nothing, but they looked around.
A full moon was rising in the sky.

They went silently up the slope, between the rocks.

“Oh man,” said Jack, “I bet they went inside a hidden cave.”
He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
He wrote: Jack turned the page.
He stared at a picture of a ninja sitting on a mat.
He read: Ninjas took orders from a ninja master.
The master was a mysterious wise person who knew many secrets of nature.
Just then the two ninjas returned.
Jack quickly put his books away.

His dolphin was taking good care of him.

Sam nodded and made clicking sounds like laughter.

I wanted you to stay calm.”
I just swam faster so you would swim faster.”

He pulled out the ocean book.
We’ll never be Master Librarians now.”

Rough and gray as a rock—” “And plain as plain can be!”

He opened the soaked ocean book.

In this way, over a few years, a pearl is formed.

Jack pushed his glasses into place.
Then he and Annie picked up their shoes and socks.
They climbed through the window of the tree house.
Morgan’s scroll was lying on the floor.
She and Jack stared at the scroll.
In its place was one shimmering silver word: OYSTER “Morgan’s magic,” whispered Annie.
Jack let out a huge sigh.
“And here’s the Pennsylvania book,” said Annie.
She pointed to a picture of the Frog Creek woods.
The tree house started to spin.
The wind blew harder and harder.
Dawn light slanted into the tree house.
No time at all had passed since they’d left.
Jack rolled up the ancient scroll.
He tucked it into the corner.
“We solved the first riddle,” he said.
“I don’t see another scroll,” said Annie.
“Maybe tomorrow we’ll get the next riddle.”

His T-shirt and shorts were still soaked.
Only his shoes and socks were dry.
“And this needs to dry out, too,” said Annie.
She put the wet ocean book in a patch of sunlight.
Then Jack and Annie climbed down the ladder.
They walked through the woods, through leafy shadows and golden light.
They left the woods and started down their street.
“You know, we should have found the answer to the riddle right away,” said Jack.
“The oyster was on the reef all along.”
“I know, but we wouldn’t have had so much fun,” said Annie.

“Don’t forget the dolphins,” Annie said simply.
The dolphins made up for everything.
“I guess they were the true pearl in the oyster,” said Annie.
“I wonder what Sam is doing right now.”
They climbed their steps and went into their house.
Then he and Annie slipped up the stairs to change their clothes.

“Just two more to go,” she whispered.
He pulled out Days of the Wild West.
He put it on top of a stack of books.
Annie was staring at the books.
Annie pointed at the Wild West book.
He read the title aloud: “Days of the Wild West.”
The author’s name was below the title.
He and Annie stared at the words for a long moment.
The book he wrote after he left us!”
Jack and Annie shook their heads with wonder.
He looked at the title page.
At the bottom of the page, he read: Texas Press, Dallas, 1895.
He read the dedication: WITH THANKS TO SMILEY AND SHORTY, TWO STRANGERS WHO CHANGED MY LIFE Jack looked at Annie.
“Slim dedicated his book to us,” he said.
Jack placed Slim’s book back on the stack of books.
Then he and Annie left the tree house and climbed down the ladder.
As they started through the woods, the trees were alive with bird sounds.
The air felt soft and moist.
“Frog Creek seems so peaceful,” said Jack.
“Yeah, but no Slim Cooley, either,” said Annie sadly.
“But when we read his book, it’s like he’s still talking to us.”
“You mean it’s like an echo from the past?”
Just then, out of the blue, a voice called, “Jack!
Then they ran all the way home, through the long shadows of the setting sun.
From this valley they say you are going.
I shall miss your sweet face and bright smile.
For they say you are taking the sunshine That has brightened my pathway awhile.
Refrain (after each verse): Come and sit by my side if you love me.
Do not hasten to bid me adieu.
For remember the Red River Valley And the cowboy who loved you so true.
There never could be such a longing In the heart of a poor cowboy’s breast.
As dwells in this heart you are breaking While I wait in my home in the West.
Do you think of this valley you’re leaving, Oh, how lonely and dreary it will be?
Do you think of the kind hearts you’re grieving, And the pain you are causing to me?
From this valley they say you are going.
I will miss your bright eyes and sweet smile.
For they say you are weary and tired And must find a new range for a while.
Come and sit by my side if you love me.
Do not hasten to bid me adieu,
for remember the Red River Valley and the cowboy who loved you so.
